name: Djambarrpuyŋu
confidence_why: Wilkinson's 1991 reference grammar places primary stress on the first syllable of every word and Jepson's 2019 acoustic study confirms that the initial syllable carries the word's prominence (Jepson, Fletcher and Stoakes 2021 and Jepson 2025 restate the same placement), the only disagreement being that Jepson 2019 finds no acoustic evidence for the secondary stresses Wilkinson described.

new_statements.quote: Djambarrpuyŋu, like all previously described Australian languages, is classified as having lexical stress. Stress in Djambarrpuyŋu is largely predictable (Wilkinson, 2012). Primary, or main stress occurs on the initial syllable of a word. Secondary stress is assigned to the initial syllable of subsequent "stress groups." Stress groups consist of two or three syllables and are treated as the structural core to the metrical structure system in the Yolngu languages. As is found to be the case for many Australian languages, stress assignment in Djambarrpuyŋu (after Wilkinson, 2012) is affected by morpheme boundaries with the initial syllable of suffixing morphemes analyzed as attracting a secondary lexical prominence. The initial syllable of words is further defined as the tonic syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog initial stress = fixed initial stress for all word lengths; the paper states primary stress on the initial syllable of a word, so the placement agrees. It refines with secondary-stress groups, morpheme-conditioned secondary stress, and final-syllable extrametricality. The paper is a phonetic study of consonant duration; the stress statement is a summary of Wilkinson (2012), not an independent finding. The listed open_url (Auckland ResearchSpace hdl:2292/46817) is a bot-challenge landing page and the DSpace API reports accessStatus 'restricted' with bundles hidden; the same postprint was downloaded from Melbourne's Minerva Access (hdl 11343/297126, accessStatus open.access).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word (following Wilkinson 2012). Secondary stresses fall on the initial syllable of each subsequent two- or three-syllable 'stress group', and the first syllable of a suffixing morpheme attracts a secondary stress (morpheme boundaries reset the count). The word-initial syllable is also the tonic syllable, the docking site of the phrasal pitch accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, per the phonological description: on the initial syllable of each subsequent stress group (2-3 syllables) and on the initial syllable of suffixing morphemes. Footnote 3 (p. 25): 'word-final syllables are generally treated as extrametrical for stress assignment. This means word-final syllables are not stressed unless the word is monosyllabic, the word is a compound and the second member is monosyllabic, or if a monosyllabic form is reduplicated. In the latter two cases, this may also result in stress falling on adjacent syllables.' The paper also reports (p. 7) that a preliminary acoustic study found no vowel lengthening in primary stressed vs unstressed syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final syllables extrametrical (never stressed) except in monosyllables, compounds whose second member is monosyllabic, and reduplicated monosyllables, where adjacent syllables may both bear stress (fn. 3, p. 25). Footnote 2 (p. 25): Wilkinson's analysis follows Wood (1978) on Gaalpu and Waters (1979) on Djinang, two distantly related Yolngu languages.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Djambarrpuyŋu as spoken at Galiwin'ku (Elcho Island), the variety of Wilkinson's (1991/2012) grammar; the 2021 paper notes (fn. 2) that Wilkinson's stress analysis follows Wood (1978) on Gaalpu and Waters (1979) on Djinang, two other Yolngu languages, and mentions Gupapuyŋu as a closely related variety.

new_statements.quote: Wilkinson (2012, p. 62) states that "[s]tress patterning in Djambarrpuyŋu is largely predictable", with the first syllable being primary stressed. (p. 14) ... There was no support for word-internal prominences assigned rhythmically or by morphological structure that had previously been proposed by (Wilkinson, 2012). It therefore appears that there is support for two levels of word stress in Djambarrpuyŋu: primary stress on the initial syllable of words, and unstressed which is assigned to all other syllables. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable (its only consistent acoustic correlate is the highest f0 in the word, carried by the phrasal pitch accent; duration, intensity and vowel quality do not distinguish it). Acoustic analysis finds no evidence for the secondary stresses on alternating syllables or suffix-initial syllables that Wilkinson (2012) proposed; the thesis concludes there are two levels only, initial primary stress and unstressed elsewhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Previously described (Wilkinson 2012) on alternating odd syllables / suffix-initial syllables, but the thesis finds no phonetic evidence for it (abstract p. iv: 'evidence for secondary stress, considered for both morpheme internal and morpheme initial secondary stresses is not found'; p. 299: 'Word-internal vowels in putatively secondary stressed syllables were not found to be acoustically differentiated from their unstressed counterparts').
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the extrametricality of final syllables inherited from Wilkinson; the thesis's own finding is the absence of measurable secondary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Djambarrpuyŋu as spoken at Galiwin'ku (Elcho Island), the variety of Wilkinson's (1991/2012) grammar; the 2021 paper notes (fn. 2) that Wilkinson's stress analysis follows Wood (1978) on Gaalpu and Waters (1979) on Djinang, two other Yolngu languages, and mentions Gupapuyŋu as a closely related variety.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on primary stress placement: the catalog, Jepson-Fletcher-Stoakes 2021 (citing Wilkinson 2012) and Jepson's 2019 thesis all put main stress on the word-initial syllable. The only tension concerns secondary stress: the 2021 paper repeats Wilkinson's description of secondary stresses on the initial syllable of each 2-3 syllable stress group and of suffixing morphemes, whereas the 2019 thesis (the acoustic study the paper draws on) finds no phonetic evidence for any secondary stress and proposes a two-level system (initial primary stress vs unstressed); the paper itself notes that non-pitch correlates of primary stress are also absent.
